title: Nobel Medicine Prize Awarded for Brain Research
paragraphs: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded to three scientists whose discoveries have transformed the study of the brain. The prize was announced in October 2026 by the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.

The prize was shared by Karl Deisseroth, a 54-year-old American scientist at Stanford University, and two German researchers: Peter Hegemann, 71, of Humboldt University in Berlin, and Georg Nagel, 73, of the University of Würzburg. They were honored "for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics," and they will share prize money of 12 million Swedish crowns, which is approximately 1.2 million dollars.

Optogenetics is a technique that makes it possible to switch individual nerve cells in a living brain on or off using light. Its origins can be traced back to research by Hegemann and Nagel on a single-celled green alga called Chlamydomonas. These tiny organisms are able to sense light and swim toward it. The researchers discovered that this ability depends on a light-sensitive protein, which became known as channelrhodopsin. When light strikes this protein, it opens a channel that allows electrically charged particles to flow into the cell.

Deisseroth and his colleagues later realized that this protein could be used as a powerful research tool. By inserting the gene that produces channelrhodopsin into specific nerve cells in the brains of laboratory animals, scientists could make those cells respond to light. As a result, they could activate or silence particular groups of neurons with remarkable precision, simply by shining light on them, and then observe the effects on the animals' behavior.

This breakthrough has enabled researchers to investigate how particular brain circuits control behavior, emotions and memory, a task that had previously been extremely difficult. According to the Nobel committee, the method is now being used in laboratories around the world and is helping to reveal the brain's mysteries. Scientists have used it to study conditions such as anxiety, depression and addiction, as well as how memories are formed.

Optogenetics has also begun to be explored as a medical treatment. For example, researchers have tested the approach as a way to partially restore vision in people with certain types of inherited blindness, although such uses are still at an early stage.
